GEO-TREES Tree Inventory Data Processing Workflow

1 Introduction

This purpose of this vignette is to demonstrate and document the complete workflow for processing tree inventory data for the GEO-TREES initiative. The code in this vignette matches the code in the R scripts elsewhere in this repository. For automated processing of GEO-TREES tree inventory data it is recommended to run the R scripts directly, not to use this vignette. This vignette includes additional data visualisations to help understand how the data is processed, and may provide a useful guide when processing a site for the first time. Throughout the vignette there are sign-posts to the relevant R script in the automated workflow.

Key steps of the workflow:

  • Format raw field data to match the GEO-TREES L0 data format
  • Align taxonomic names for each stem measurement
  • Estimate height, wood density, and above-ground woody biomass of tree stems
  • Fit spatial polygons for each plot
  • Calculate summary statistics of forest structure and biomass stocks within 50x50 m quadrats

This vignette uses an anonymised dataset, based on real data from a tropical wet forest site in South America. To illustrate the use of all supported auxiliary datasets and processing steps, some synthetic data have been generated.

Synthetic data are provided for:

  • Locally-measured wood density estimates
  • Locally-measured tree height estimates
  • Local biomass and height allometries

indir <- "./data-raw/data"

3 Create L0 data

This part of the workflow will vary among sites, depending on the structure of the raw field data. Consult the GEO-TREES Tree Inventory Data Collection Guidelines Section 16: Data format for information on the GEO-TREES L0 data format. The current repository also contains template files for formatting raw data, in the ./templates/ folder.

We provide various functions to help create valid GEO-TREES L0 data products:

  • pasteVals() intelligently pastes values together, replacing NAs with blanks, useful for combining values in the code column.
  • colGen() creates empty columns in a dataframe if they don’t already exist, using a spec. table.
  • colCheck() checks whether the columns in a dataframe exactly match those in a spec. table based on their name and class (e.g. numeric, character).
  • valCheck() runs a series of simple logical checks on the different GEO-TREES Tree Inventory L0 data objects.

You can see various examples of R scripts used to transform raw field data into L0 data in ./sites/<SITE NAME>/<ACQUISITION ID>/01_fmt.R.

4 Specify processing parameters

Choices made during the processing workflow, for example the choice to use a local or regional height-diameter estimation method, should be specified in a param.yaml YAML configuration file. This file also defines some site meta-data and filepaths.

There should be one param.yaml file for each version of the processed data.

param.yaml files should contain the following parameters:

  • site_id – Name of the site, e.g. "Bicuar"
  • acquisition_id – ID of data acquisition, e.g. "2024"
  • out_dir – Path to where processed data will be exported, e.g. "./dat/sites/Bicuar/INV/2024/v1"
  • raw_dir – Path to the raw input data, e.g. "./dat/sites/Bicuar/INV/2024/L0"
  • raw_version – Version of the raw input data, a sub-directory of raw_dir, e.g. "v1". When raw data are corrected, create a new version so that previous outputs can still be reproduced
  • s3_dir – Optional, path to AWS S3 directory containing raw input data, e.g. "johngodlee/GEO-TREES_INV/dat/sites/Amacayacu/INV/2024/L0"
  • quad_dim – Dimensions in metres of quadrats, e.g. [50, 50] for 50x50 m square quadrats
  • opt_s3 – Boolean (true/false). If true, raw input data will be pulled from an AWS S3 bucket specified in s3_dir, otherwise a local directory specified in raw_dir
  • product_version – String specifying the version of the data products, e.g. "v1". Data products may be specified with different parameter sets, for example different size quadrats (quad_dim) or different methods of estimating stem height (height_method).
  • software_version – String specifying the version of the code used to generate the data products, normally a GitHub release version, e.g. "v2.4"
  • height_method – Method used to estimate stem height, either "regional" or "field"
  • wd_method – Method used to estimate wood density, either "regional" or "field"
  • polygon_method – Method used to fit plot polygons, one of "exact", "affine" or "procrustes", see Fit plot spatial polygons
  • outside_max_dist_m – Maximum distance in metres outside the quadrat grid at which stems are assigned to the nearest quadrat, e.g. 5. 0 excludes all stems outside the grid from quadrat summaries
  • corner_outlier_dist_m – Maximum distance in metres between a measured plot corner and the fitted plot polygon, beyond which the corner is treated as an outlier, e.g. 10, see Fit plot spatial polygons
  • quad_grid_tol – Maximum proportion of the area of each plot which may be excluded from the grid of quadrats, e.g. 0.1. The automated workflow centres the quadrat grid in each plot, so where the plot dimensions are not a multiple of the quadrat dimensions, equal strips along opposite edges of the plot are excluded, e.g. 0.4 allows 100 x 100 m quadrats in a 250 x 250 m plot, which excludes 36% of the plot
  • height_model – Height-diameter model used if height_method is "field", one of "best" (lowest residual standard error), "log1", "log2", "weibull" or "michaelis"
  • agbd_diam_min_cm – Minimum stem diameter in cm for AGB density. The larger of this and the minimum diameter threshold of each plot is used, e.g. 0 uses the threshold of each plot
  • include_broken – true or false, whether stems broken above the POM are included in AGB density
  • multi_stem_method – How AGB is estimated for multi-stemmed trees, either "equivalent" (from the equivalent diameter of a single stem with the same basal area as the tree) or "stem" (from each stem separately)
  • unmapped_method – How trees without stem coordinates are treated, either "random" (assigned to a random quadrat in their plot in each Monte Carlo simulation) or "exclude" (excluded from AGB density)
  • diam_error – Diameter measurement error propagated to AGB, either "chave2004" (Chave et al. 2004), "field" (estimated from repeat diameter measurements in stem_dup.csv with BIOMASS::fitDiamError()), "none", or a number giving the standard deviation of diameter measurement error in cm
  • quad_origin – Optional, alignment of the quadrat grid in each plot: "centre" (default) centres the grid in the plot, "corner" starts it at the origin corner of the plot, and [x, y] starts it x and y m from the origin corner. Where the plot dimensions are not a multiple of the quadrat dimensions, strips of the plot outside the grid are left out
  • als_date – Optional, date of the airborne lidar acquisition matched to the plot data, "YYYY-MM-DD", "YYYY-MM" or "YYYY", used to report the time between the ALS acquisition and the census in 12_report.R
  • rocrate – Information on who ran the workflow, used in the RO-Crate meta-data files which accompany each data product:
    • author_name – e.g. "John L. Godlee"
    • author_email – e.g. "GodleeJ@si.edu"
    • author_orcid – Optional, ORCID URL of the author, e.g. "https://orcid.org/0000-0000-0000-0000"
    • affiliation – e.g. "Smithsonian Institution"
    • license – License file for the data products, e.g. "TERMS.md"

Import the example param.yaml:

Show code 
# Import param.yaml
# p <- yaml::read_yaml("./sites/<SITE>/<ACQUISITION>/<PRODUCTVERSION>/param.yaml")
p <- read_yaml(file.path(indir, "param.yaml"))

# Import software version
software_version <- read_yaml(file.path(indir, "version.yaml"))

# Merge parameters lists
param <- c(p, software_version)

# Define parameter names
param_name_vec <- c(
  "site_id",
  "acquisition_id",
  "quad_dim",
  "opt_s3",
  "s3_dir",
  "out_dir",
  "raw_dir",
  "raw_version",
  "height_method",
  "wd_method",
  "polygon_method",
  "outside_max_dist_m",
  "corner_outlier_dist_m",
  "quad_grid_tol",
  "height_model",
  "agbd_diam_min_cm",
  "include_broken",
  "multi_stem_method",
  "unmapped_method",
  "diam_error",
  "software_version",
  "product_version",
  "rocrate"
)

# Define RO-Crate parameter names, `author_orcid` is optional
rocrate_name_vec <- c(
  "author_name",
  "author_email",
  "affiliation",
  "license"
)

# Check all parameters present
# `s3_dir` is only needed if `opt_s3` is TRUE
param_missing <- setdiff(param_name_vec, names(param))
if (isFALSE(param$opt_s3)) {
  param_missing <- setdiff(param_missing, "s3_dir")
}
if (length(param_missing) > 0) {
  stop("Missing parameters: ", paste(param_missing, collapse = ", "))
}

rocrate_missing <- setdiff(rocrate_name_vec, names(param$rocrate))
if (length(rocrate_missing) > 0) {
  stop("Missing `rocrate` parameters: ", paste(rocrate_missing, collapse = ", "))
}

# Check parameter values
param_choices <- list(
  height_method = c("regional", "field"),
  wd_method = c("regional", "field"),
  polygon_method = c("exact", "affine", "procrustes"),
  height_model = c("best", "log1", "log2", "weibull", "michaelis"),
  multi_stem_method = c("equivalent", "stem"),
  unmapped_method = c("random", "exclude")
)
for (i in names(param_choices)) {
  if (!param[[i]] %in% param_choices[[i]]) {
    stop("`", i, "` must be one of: ", paste(param_choices[[i]], collapse = ", "))
  }
}

# Optional parameters
if (is.null(param$quad_origin)) {
  param$quad_origin <- "centre"
}

# Print parameters
param

If opt_s3 is true, the paws package should be loaded to allow data data to be retrieved from an AWS S3 bucket. This is only relevant if data processing is happening on the MAAP platform.

Show code 
# Optionally load AWS S3 package
if (param$opt_s3) {
  library(paws)
}

5 Data structure

GEO-TREES data products are organised in a strict directory hierarchy:

  • SITE - The site name. Matches the site_id column in tree inventory datasets.
  • DATATYPE - in this case “INV” tree inventory data. Alternatively, e.g. “ALS” (airborne laser scanning) or “TLS” (terrestrial laser scanning)
  • ACQUISITION - The ID of the discrete period when L0 data was acquired in the field using a particular platform, normally including the date of acquisition in YYYY-MM-DD format. Where a L0 dataset was acquired over multiple days, prefer the mid-acquisition date. Tree inventory acquisitions are named by census year, i.e. the year of the mid-date of all stem measurements, in YYYY format.
  • PRODUCT - Data product level, either:
    • “L0” - raw data
    • “L1” - re-formatted raw data (raw instrument)
    • “L2” - model-derived products at matching resolution of L1
    • “L3” - variables mapped to uniform space-time grid scales
  • PRODUCTVERSION - Version of the code used to produce the data product, normally a GitHub release version of the code used to produce that data product.

Not all data products must utilise all levels of the directory hierarchy, and certain products may include additional levels where specified, but the order of the basic hierarchy does not change. This directory structure means that sub-directory levels are never mixed within a parent directory. See below for a breakdown of these levels:

Data product files are named according to the full directory hierarchy, with levels separated by underscores (_), and a consistent suffix across files of a given type within a product. Thus, hierarchy levels should not contain underscores (“_”). To prevent interference with file extensions, hierarchy levels should also not contain dots (periods, “.”). Both these characters should be replaced with a hyphen (“-”). For example, for the tree inventory (INV) L3 quadrat-level AGBD estimates for site “PanamaCanal”, acquired on the 1st January 2025, processed using version 2.4 of the tree inventory processing pipeline, using the v2 parameter set:

SITE: PanamaCanal DATATYPE: INV ACQUISITION: 2025-01-01 PRODUCTVERSION: v2 SOFTWAREVERSION: v2.4 PRODUCT: L3 File: quad

Directory path: PanamaCanal/INV/2025-01-01/v2/v2-4/L3/ Filename: PanamaCanal_INV_2025-01-01_v2_v2-4_L3_quad.gpkg

6 Import L0 data

For convenience, we create a list L0 where each element is a different L0 tree inventory data object. Column classes are taken from the column templates in ./templates/, so that e.g. an acquisition_id of "2024" is read as a character string rather than a number.

Show code 
# Import column classes from column templates
colClass <- function(x) {
  cols <- read.csv(file.path("../../templates", paste0(x, "_cols.csv")))
  setNames(cols$class, cols$column_name)
}

# Import raw L0 data
L0 <- list(
  # Import stem measurements
  stem = read.csv(file.path(indir, "stem.csv"), colClasses = colClass("stem")),

  # Import plot meta-data
  plot = read.csv(file.path(indir, "plot.csv"), colClasses = colClass("plot")),

  # Import plot geo-location data
  pt = read.csv(file.path(indir, "pt.csv"), colClasses = colClass("pt")),

  # Import taxonomy data (optional)
  taxa = read.csv(file.path(indir, "taxa.csv"), colClasses = colClass("taxon")),

  # Import individual local wood density estimates (optional)
  wd = read.csv(file.path(indir, "wd.csv"), colClasses = colClass("wd")),

  # Import additional height-diameter measurements (optional)
  height = read.csv(file.path(indir, "hd.csv"), colClasses = colClass("height"))
)

If you are on the MAAP platform and data is stored in an S3 bucket, use this method to copy the files to a local directory first.

Show code 
# If S3, copy raw data from S3 bucket to local directory
if (param$opt_s3) {
  # Get object list from S3
  s3_client <- s3(region = "us-west-2")

  # Define S3 bucket where MAAP user directories are located
  # YOU MAY NEED CHANGE THIS
  bucket <- "maap-ops-workspace"

  # Identify files in dir_input
  s3_response <- s3_client$list_objects_v2(Bucket = bucket, Prefix = param$s3_dir)

  # Collect S3 paths from bucket
  shared_objects <- sapply(s3_response$Contents, "[[", "Key")

  # Check files detected
  if (length(shared_objects) == 0) { 
    stop("No raw data files detected in S3 bucket")
  }
  
  # Retrieve all files
  for (i in shared_objects) {
    # Construct new key in destination folder
    dest_key <- sub(param$s3_dir, param$raw_dir, i)

    # Copy files to local directory
    s3_client$download_file(Bucket = bucket, Key = i, Filename = dest_key)
  }
}

The stem measurement table contains one row per stem measurement. Stems may be measured multiple times within a single census, for example if multiple diameter measurements are collected at different Points of Measurement (POMs) along the length of the stem.

The record_id column is a unique identifier for the stem measurement record within the site, essentially the row number of the stem measurement table.

The measurement_date column records the date of each measurement as a decimal year, e.g. 2024.585 for 2nd August 2024, and measurement_date_res records the resolution of the original date: "YYYY-MM-DD", "YYYY-MM", or "YYYY". The decDate() function converts dates to decimal years. Dates recorded only to the month or year are placed at the middle of that month or year, e.g. decDate("2024") returns 2024.5.

The plot meta-data table contains one row per census per plot. It contains additional information on field methodology, and qualitative information on local environmental conditions and vegetation structure. These data are used mostly for interpretation.

The plot geo-location table contains one row per location estimate of a single survey point. Survey points may have multiple location estimates which are then averaged when fitting the plot polygon. This table contains many columns reserved for additional information provided when differential GNSS equipment is used. In the example dataset these columns are blank ebcause the survey points were collected with a single handheld GNSS unit.

The optional taxa table contains additional taxonomic information. Each row is a taxonomic name that features in the stem table, and columns contain corrected taxonomic name information. This table is only used for interpretation. It is useful in the case where codes or short-hand taxonomic names were used in the field and those need to be linked with the full taxonomic name.

The optional wood density table contains local field-measured wood density. These measurements do not have to come from the plots, or even the same site, but should be representative of the trees in the site. Each row is a taxonomic name that features in the stem table. Where multiple wood density measurements were collected for a single taxon, these should be aggregated to a mean, standard deviation and the number of measurements.

The optional stem height table contains local field-measured stem diameter and height measurements. These measurements do not have to come from the plots, or even the same site, but should be representative of the trees in the site. In this case, the measurements were colelcted within the same site, but outside the plots, hence the site_id column is filled, but the plot_id column is filled with NA values.

Before processing, valCheck() runs a series of checks on the L0 data objects. It returns an error for values which would cause the processing to fail, or which are impossible, e.g. negative stem diameters, plot IDs which don’t match between tables, or values outside the ranges given in the template files in ./templates/. It returns a warning for values which are probably wrong, but which may be legitimate, e.g. stems mapped far outside the plot, or stems without a stem_id.

Show code 
# Check values in L0 data
valCheck(
  plot = L0$plot,
  stem = L0$stem,
  pt = L0$pt,
  taxon = L0$taxa,
  height = L0$height,
  wd = L0$wd)

7 Correct taxonomy

02_taxa.R

Here we combine all the taxonomic names recorded across all the L0 data objects, then use the BIOMASS::correctTaxo() function to query the World Flora Online (WFO) API to find matching taxonomic names in their database.

The argument interactive = TRUE means that when a name matches multiple taxonomic names in the WFO database, users will be prompted to pick the correct taxonomic name from a list in the R console. In the automated workflow, prompts are only shown in an interactive R session. When processing many sites with zz_site_all.R, which sets options(inv.batch = TRUE), ambiguous names are left unmatched so that processing isn’t interrupted. These names can be matched in a later interactive run.

Example of the interactive dialogue returned by correctTaxo() for the name "Julbernardia pan":

> Enter a number to pick a row from the list, a valid WFO ID, 'N' for the next page, 'P' for the previous page, 'S' or press Enter to skip:

In the example dataset the taxonomic names are strings containing the genus, species, any infra-specific epithets such as variety (var.) or subspecies (subsp.), or a higher-order taxonomic rank such as just the genus or family. Some examples of valid names:

  • “Burkea africana”
  • “Pseudolachnostylis maprouneifolia var. glabra”
  • “Quercus”
  • “Fagaceae”

correctTaxo() also allows the user to pass separate genus and species (species epithet) columns if your data is formatted that way.

If useCache = TRUE, correctTaxo() creates a cache object containing previously queried taxonomic names, including the choices made during interactive matching. In the automated workflow this cache is saved with the raw data, to wfo_cache.rds in the directory containing raw_dir, e.g. ./dat/sites/<SITE>/INV/<ACQUISITION>/wfo_cache.rds. It is shared by all product versions of an acquisition, as a record of the choices made. Names are matched in chunks, and the cache is saved after each chunk, so choices are kept if interactive matching is interrupted. Names which could not be matched in a batch run are not saved, so they are offered again in the next interactive run.

Show code 
# Combine taxa across tables
taxon_vec <- sort(unique(c(
  L0$stem$taxon_name,
  L0$wd$taxon_name,
  L0$height$taxon_name)))

# Load WFO cache from previous processing
loadWFOCache(file.path(indir, "wfo_cache.rds"))

# Prompt the user only in interactive sessions
taxa_interactive <- interactive() && !isTRUE(getOption("inv.batch"))

# Match names in chunks, saving the cache after each chunk
# In the vignette the cache is saved to a temporary file
wfo_path <- file.path(tempdir(), "wfo_cache.rds")
chunk_size <- 25
taxon_chunks <- split(taxon_vec, ceiling(seq_along(taxon_vec) / chunk_size))
taxa_list <- list()
for (i in seq_along(taxon_chunks)) {
  taxa_list[[i]] <- BIOMASS::correctTaxo(
    genus = taxon_chunks[[i]], 
    species = NULL,
    interactive = taxa_interactive, 
    preferAccepted = TRUE,
    preferFuzzy = FALSE,
    sub_pattern = subPattern(),
    useCache = TRUE,
    useAPI = TRUE,
    capacity = 60,
    fill_time_s = 1, 
    timeout = 60)

  saveWFOCache(wfo_path, rm_empty = !taxa_interactive)
}
stem_taxa_all <- bind_rows(taxa_list)
Show code 
# Inspect taxa table
kable(head(stem_taxa_all))

To make it easier to check the results, we create a table of names which were changed (e.g. synonyms, spelling corrections) or which could not be matched, with the method used to match each name and the number of stems affected. In the automated workflow this table is written to report/taxa_review.csv. Methods include "AUTO" (a single exact match), "AUTO ACC" (the only accepted name among several candidates), "MANUAL" (picked by the user), "SKIP" (skipped by the user), and "EMPTY" (no match found).

Show code 
# Create table of names which were changed or not matched, for review
taxa_method <- vapply(stem_taxa_all$nameSubmitted, function(x) { 
  m <- BIOMASS::getWFOCache()[[x]]$method
  if (is.null(m) || is.na(x)) NA_character_ else m
}, character(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE)

# Names are compared ignoring case and repeated whitespace
nameStd <- function(x) tolower(trimws(gsub("\\s+", " ", x)))

taxa_review <- stem_taxa_all %>%
  mutate(
    method = taxa_method,
    n_stem = as.vector(table(L0$stem$taxon_name)[nameOriginal]),
    n_stem = ifelse(is.na(n_stem), 0L, n_stem)) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(nameOriginal), nameOriginal != "",
    is.na(nameAccepted) | nameStd(nameOriginal) != nameStd(nameAccepted)) %>%
  dplyr::select(nameOriginal, nameAccepted, familyAccepted, method, n_stem) %>%
  arrange(is.na(nameAccepted), desc(n_stem))

8 Estimate stem wood density

03_wd.R

Here we estimate the wood density of each stem measurement using the BIOMASS::getWoodDensity() function, which uses taxonomic names to extract wood density estimates at species, genus, or family level. These estimates are provided by BIOMASS, from models fitted to version 2 of the Global Wood Density Database (Zanne et al. 2009). Stems of taxa which are not in the database are given the mean wood density of their plot.

Show code 
# Join taxonomy data to stem data
taxa_all <- left_join(L0$stem, stem_taxa_all, by = c("taxon_name" = "nameOriginal"))

In the example dataset there are local field-measured wood density estimates that we can use. For getWoodDensity() to use them we need to summarise individual measurements to the mean and standard deviation of each taxon. We summarise by the accepted taxonomic name, so that different original names which refer to the same taxon are pooled. Measurements without a wood density value are excluded.

Show code 
# Optionally process local wood density data
wd_summ <- L0$wd %>%
  left_join(., stem_taxa_all, by = c("taxon_name" = "nameOriginal")) %>% 
  filter(!is.na(genusAccepted), !is.na(wood_density_gcm3)) %>% 
  mutate(wood_density_n = ifelse(is.na(wood_density_n), 1, wood_density_n)) %>% 
  group_by(
    family = familyAccepted, 
    genus = genusAccepted, 
    species = speciesAccepted) %>%
  summarise(
    wood_density_n_total = sum(wood_density_n),
    meanWD = sum(wood_density_gcm3 * wood_density_n) / wood_density_n_total,
    sdWD = {
      # If SD is NA, treat as 0 (no variance) 
      # but still account distance from grand mean
      clean_sd = ifelse(is.na(wood_density_sd_gcm3), 0, wood_density_sd_gcm3)
      
      # Components for grand variance
      ss_within  = sum((wood_density_n - 1) * clean_sd^2)
      ss_between = sum(wood_density_n * (wood_density_gcm3 - meanWD)^2)
      
      # If wood_density_n_total <= 1, return NA; otherwise calculate SD
      if (wood_density_n_total > 1) {
        sqrt((ss_within + ss_between) / (wood_density_n_total - 1)) 
      } else {
        NA_real_
      }
    },
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>% 
  dplyr::select(family, genus, species, meanWD, sdWD)

Then we estimate the wood density of each stem. Where a taxon has a local wood density estimate with no standard deviation, e.g. from a single sample, and is not in the Global Wood Density Database, we fill the missing standard deviation with the mean standard deviation of other taxa estimated at the same taxonomic level. Without a standard deviation, these stems would be dropped from the AGB error propagation.

Show code 
# Estimate wood density for each stem measurement
wd_all <- BIOMASS::getWoodDensity(
  genus = taxa_all$genusAccepted, 
  species = taxa_all$speciesAccepted,
  stand = taxa_all$plot_id,
  family = taxa_all$familyAccepted,
  addWoodDensityData = if (param$wd_method == "field") { wd_summ },
  verbose = TRUE)

# Check rows of output match stems
stopifnot(
  nrow(wd_all) == nrow(taxa_all),
  identical(as.character(wd_all$genus), as.character(taxa_all$genusAccepted)),
  identical(as.character(wd_all$species), as.character(taxa_all$speciesAccepted)))

# Fill missing wood density SD with the mean SD of other taxa estimated at the
# same level
sd_na <- is.na(wd_all$sdWD)
if (any(sd_na)) {
  sd_level <- wd_all %>% 
    filter(!is.na(sdWD)) %>% 
    distinct(genus, species, levelWD, sdWD) %>% 
    group_by(levelWD) %>% 
    summarise(sdWD_fill = mean(sdWD), .groups = "drop")
  sd_fill <- sd_level$sdWD_fill[match(wd_all$levelWD[sd_na], sd_level$levelWD)]
  sd_fill[is.na(sd_fill)] <- mean(sd_level$sdWD_fill)
  wd_all$sdWD[sd_na] <- sd_fill
}

# Create output dataframe
stem_wd_all <- cbind(record_id = taxa_all$record_id, wd_all)
Show code 
# Inspect output
kable(head(stem_wd_all))

9 Estimate stem height

04_height.R

Here we estimate the height of each stem measurement. Height estimates are required for most stem AGB allometries.

There are multiple approaches to estimating stem height. In general, we recommend this approach:

If there is an appropriate existing local height-diameter allometry, use that to estimate the height of all stems in the site. A local height-diameter allometry is deemed appropriate if the underlying data approximately span the range of stem heights measured in the tree inventory data, the species composition is similar to that found in the tree inventory data, and the local conditions (water availability, temperature, topography) of the location where the underlying data were collected are similar to that of the GEO-TREES site.

Otherwise if there is no existing local height-diameter allometry available, if you have at least 50 local and reliable estimates of stem height and diameter, spanning the range of stem size across the plots, fit a local height-diameter allometry using the BIOMASS::modelHD() function.

Finally, if neither of the above are appropriate, use the BIOMASS::retrieveH() function and supply plot coordinates to estimate stem height from a regional height-diameter allometry (Chave et al. 2014).

# Compare height diameter models
height_mod_comp <- modelHD(
  D = L0$height$diam_cm,
  H = L0$height$height_m,
  bayesian = FALSE,
  useCache = FALSE,
  drawGraph = TRUE)
Show code 
# Inspect tabular output of modelHD()
kable(height_mod_comp)
Example of output of BIOMASS::modelHD() model fit comparison table.
method RSE RSElog Average_bias
log1 3.353 0.3167 0.0190

Show code 
# Choose height diameter model, set by `height_model`. If "best", use the
# model with the lowest residual standard error, calculated on the
# untransformed height scale for all models, so comparable across log and
# non-log models
height_mod_best <- if (param$height_model == "best") {
  height_mod_comp$method[which.min(height_mod_comp$RSE)]
} else {
  param$height_model
}

# Fit best height diameter model
height_mod <- modelHD(
  D = L0$height$diam_cm,
  H = L0$height$height_m,
  method = height_mod_best,
  bayesian = FALSE,
  useCache = FALSE,
  drawGraph = TRUE)
Show code 

# Predict with best height diameter model
height_est <- retrieveH(
  D = L0$stem$diam_cm,
  model = height_mod)

# Create output dataframe
stem_height_all <- L0$stem %>% 
  mutate(
    height_m_pred = height_est$H,
    height_m_pred_rse = height_est$RSE) %>% 
  dplyr::select(record_id, height_m_pred, height_m_pred_rse)

We choose the model with the lowest residual standard error (RSE). Note that Average_bias is signed, so choosing the model with the lowest Average_bias would choose the model which most underestimates stem height.

Alternatively using a regional height-diameter allometry where no height data are available. retrieveH() estimates height from Equation 6a of Chave et al. (2014), using an index of environmental stress (E) at the centre of each plot. The residual standard error of this model (0.243) is on the log scale, so it is not a standard deviation of height in metres.

Show code 
# Extract plot centres
plot_pt_split <- L0$pt %>% 
  filter(!is.na(rover_easting_utm_m), !is.na(rover_northing_utm_m)) %>% 
  split(., .$crs_epsg)
p_cent <- bind_rows(lapply(plot_pt_split, function(x) { 
  st_as_sf(x, coords = c("rover_easting_utm_m", "rover_northing_utm_m"), 
    crs = unique(x$crs_epsg)) %>% 
  st_transform(., 4326) 
})) %>% 
group_by(site_id, plot_id) %>% 
summarise() %>% 
st_centroid() %>% 
cbind(., st_coordinates(.)) %>% 
st_drop_geometry() %>% 
dplyr::select(plot_id, X, Y)

# Add plot centres to stem data
s_cent <- L0$stem %>% 
  left_join(., p_cent, by = "plot_id")

stopifnot(all(!is.na(s_cent$X)))
stopifnot(all(!is.na(s_cent$Y)))

# Retrieve stem heights using plot locations
height_pred <- retrieveH(
  D = s_cent$diam_cm, 
  coord = s_cent[,c("X", "Y")])

# RSE of Chave et al. (2014) Eq. 6a, on the log scale
# NOTE: not a standard deviation in metres, do not pass to AGBmonteCarlo(errH = )
height_pred$RSE <- rep(0.243, length(height_pred$H))

s_cent$height_m_pred <- height_pred$H
s_cent$height_m_pred_rse <- height_pred$RSE

# Create output dataframe
stem_height_all <- s_cent %>% 
  dplyr::select(record_id, height_m_pred, height_m_pred_rse)
Show code 
# Inspect predictions 
ggplot(s_cent, aes(x = diam_cm, y = height_m_pred)) + 
  geom_line() + 
  theme_bw() + 
  labs(
    x = "Stem diameter (cm)",
    y = "Predicted stem height (m)")

10 Estimate stem AGB

05_agb_stem.R

Here we estimate the above-ground woody biomass (AGB, agb_Mg) of each stem measurement using the BIOMASS::computeAGB() function, which returns the AGB of each tree in Mg. Where heights come from a local height-diameter model (height_method: "field"), Equation 4 from Chave et al. (2014) is used to estimate AGB with stem diameter (D), stem height (H), and wood density (WD). Where no local height data are available (height_method: "regional"), Equation 7 from Chave et al. (2014) is used, which replaces stem height with an index of environmental stress at the plot centre. This matches the allometry used in the AGB error propagation in Estimate quadrat AGBD and propagate error, so that stem-level and quadrat-level estimates are consistent. Because the Chave et al. (2014) model was fitted using mostly data from tropical wet forests, it may fail to accurately capture the relationship between stem diameter, height, and volume in other vegetation types. For these sites, a local AGB allometry may be more appropriate.

You may also choose to have different AGB allometries for different functional groups in the tree inventory data. For example, if there are large baobab trees (Adansonia sp.), bamboos, or lianas which have drastically different physiognomy to other trees in the dataset.

Where trees have multiple stems, AGB is estimated for the tree from its equivalent diameter, D_{eq} = \sqrt{\sum D_i^2}, the diameter of a single stem with the same basal area as all its stems. Estimating AGB for each stem separately would underestimate the AGB of multi-stemmed trees, because AGB increases more than proportionally with stem diameter. Tree AGB is then shared among its stems in proportion to their basal area. Trees are formed from the stems used to estimate AGB density (see Filter stem data), grouped by tree_id within each plot, using recordFilter(), agbdFilter() and treeEquiv() from func.R. Other stems, e.g. dead stems, and stems below the minimum diameter threshold of the plot, are treated as single-stemmed trees. Wood density depends on taxonomic identity, which is the same for all stems of a tree, so the wood density of the largest stem is used.

We also create some additional variables like stem basal area (ba_m2) and stem volume (volume_m3).

Show code 
# Stems which form multi-stemmed trees. If `multi_stem_method` is "stem", AGB
# is estimated for each stem separately
record_agbd <- agbdFilter(L0$stem, L0$plot, recordFilter(L0$stem, L0$plot),
  diam_min_cm = param$agbd_diam_min_cm,
  include_broken = param$include_broken)
tree_include <- if (param$multi_stem_method == "equivalent") record_agbd else character(0)

# Join wood density, height, and equivalent diameter to stem data
stem_all <- L0$stem %>%
  left_join(., stem_wd_all, by = "record_id") %>%
  left_join(., stem_height_all, by = "record_id") %>%
  left_join(., treeEquiv(L0$stem, tree_include), by = "record_id")

# One row per tree. Wood density depends on taxonomic identity, which is the
# same for all stems of a tree, so the wood density of the largest stem is used
tree <- stem_all %>%
  arrange(desc(ba_share)) %>%
  group_by(tree_key) %>%
  summarise(
    plot_id = first(plot_id),
    diam_eq_cm = first(diam_eq_cm),
    meanWD = first(meanWD),
    n_taxa = n_distinct(taxon_name),
    .groups = "drop")

if (any(tree$n_taxa > 1)) {
  warning(sum(tree$n_taxa > 1), " multi-stemmed trees have stems with ",
    "different taxonomic names. The wood density of the largest stem is used",
    call. = FALSE)
}

# Estimate tree-level AGB
if (param$height_method == "regional") {
  tree <- left_join(tree, p_cent, by = "plot_id")
  stopifnot(all(!is.na(tree$X)))
  tree$agb_Mg <- BIOMASS::computeAGB(
    D = tree$diam_eq_cm,
    WD = tree$meanWD,
    coord = as.matrix(tree[, c("X", "Y")]))
} else if (param$height_method == "field") {
  tree$agb_Mg <- BIOMASS::computeAGB(
    D = tree$diam_eq_cm,
    WD = tree$meanWD,
    H = retrieveH(D = tree$diam_eq_cm, model = height_mod)$H)
}

# Share tree AGB among stems
stem_agb_all <- stem_all %>%
  mutate(
    agb_Mg = tree$agb_Mg[match(tree_key, tree$tree_key)] * ba_share,
    ba_m2 = base::pi * (diam_cm / 2)^2 / 10000,
    volume_m3 = agb_Mg / meanWD) %>%
  dplyr::select(
    record_id,
    agb_Mg,
    ba_m2,
    volume_m3)
Show code 
# Visualise distribution of stem-level AGB
ggplot(stem_agb_all, aes(x = agb_Mg)) + 
  geom_histogram(colour = "black", fill = "grey", binwidth = 1, boundary = 0) + 
  theme_bw() + 
  labs(
    x = "Above-ground woody biomass (Mg)",
    y = "N stems")
Show code 
# Visualise relationship between basal area and AGB
ggplot(stem_agb_all, aes(x = ba_m2, y = agb_Mg)) + 
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) + 
  theme_bw() + 
  labs(
    x = expression("Basal area"~(m^2)),
    y = "Above-ground woody biomass (Mg)")

11 Filter stem data

06_record_fil.R

Here we filter the tree inventory data prior to estimating above-ground biomass density in each 50x50 m quadrat.

We apply the following filters:

  • Remove stems with no diameter measurement.
  • Include only living stems.
  • Include only standing stems.
  • Remove stems that are broken below the diameter Point of Measurement (POM). Stems broken above the POM are included.
  • Remove “missing” stems. I.e. stems which were not measured during the census.
  • Where stems were measured multiple times at multiple POMs, choose the highest POM, latest measurement date, and largest diameter measurement. Stems without a stem_id cannot be matched across measurements, so each of their records is treated as a separate stem.

Stems with a diameter below the minimum diameter threshold of the plot have their own AGB estimates, but are not part of multi-stemmed trees, and are excluded when AGB is summed to estimate AGB density, so that AGB density matches the sampling of the plot.

Show code 
# Select stems used to estimate AGB, see `recordFilter()` in func.R
# Stems without coordinates are kept, and are assigned to quadrats at random
# during AGB error propagation
record_fil <- recordFilter(L0$stem, L0$plot)

# Select stems used to estimate AGB density, see `agbdFilter()` in func.R
# Stems below the minimum diameter threshold, the larger of
# `agbd_diam_min_cm` and the threshold of the plot, are excluded. Stems broken
# above the POM are excluded if `include_broken` is false
record_agbd <- agbdFilter(L0$stem, L0$plot, record_fil,
  diam_min_cm = param$agbd_diam_min_cm,
  include_broken = param$include_broken)

12 Fit plot spatial polygons

07_quad.R

Here, we create spatial polygons representing the area of each plot, using field-measured geo-location estimates of survey points collected with GNSS devices. See the GEO-TREES Plot Geo-location Protocol for more guidance on how to collect these data. We use the BIOMASS::plotPolygonFit() function to do this.

plotPolygonFit() also projects stem map coordinates into a global coordinate reference system.

In this example we use the method = "procrustes" algorithm to fit the plot polygon, as specified by polygon_method in param.yaml, but you could also use the “affine” or “exact” methods depending on the availability and quality of the GNSS data, and the shape of the plot.

The “procrustes” method applies a rigid spatial transformation to align local field coordinates with geographic projected coordinates. The algorithm calculates the optimal two-dimensional translation (shifting) and rotation needed to best fit the local plot corners to the provided GPS measurements. Unlike the “affine” or “exact” algorithms, this method strictly preserves the internal geometry, shape, and dimensions of the original field plot, i.e. we trust the nominal dimensions of the field plot. By applying the resulting rotation matrix and translation vector uniformly to both the plot corners and the internal tree coordinates, the function ensures that all field-measured distances and spatial relationships between trees are perfectly maintained in the final geographic projection. This method is especially robust for identifying outlier GPS measurements that deviate from the rigid, known shape of the plot.

The “affine” method uses Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) linear regression to map local field coordinates to geographic coordinates. By fitting separate linear models for the X and Y axes, this method finds the optimal affine transformation, allowing for translation, rotation, independent axis scaling, and shearing that minimizes the overall squared error between the local corners and the GPS measurements. The resulting linear models are then used to predict the geographic locations of internal trees. While this method preserves parallel lines and uniform point distributions, it may alter the overall scale and internal angles of the original plot geometry.

The “exact” method requires exactly four plot corners. It determines the final geographic location of each corner by calculating the simple average of its corresponding GNSS measurements. To project the internal tree coordinates, the algorithm utilizes bilinear interpolation. It calculates the proportional distance of each tree relative to the local field corners and applies those exact proportions to the projected GPS corners. Because this method forces the plot’s corners to strictly match the averaged GPS coordinates, the internal geometry of the plot may be warped, meaning the geographic distances between projected trees may not perfectly match the distances measured in the field.

All points must share one projected coordinate reference system. If plots span more than one UTM zone, all points are transformed to the most common zone. plotPolygonFit() warns if the fitted transformation is a reflection, which usually means that the relative coordinates are mirrored, e.g. if X and Y are swapped.

Show code 
# Points must share one projected CRS. If plots span more than one UTM zone,
# transform all points to the most common zone
crs_site <- as.integer(names(which.max(table(L0$pt$crs_epsg))))
pt_fit <- L0$pt
if (length(unique(pt_fit$crs_epsg)) > 1) {
  for (i in setdiff(unique(pt_fit$crs_epsg), crs_site)) {
    sel <- pt_fit$crs_epsg == i & 
      !is.na(pt_fit$rover_easting_utm_m) & !is.na(pt_fit$rover_northing_utm_m)
    xy <- st_coordinates(st_transform(
      st_as_sf(pt_fit[sel, ], 
        coords = c("rover_easting_utm_m", "rover_northing_utm_m"), crs = i), 
      crs_site))
    pt_fit$rover_easting_utm_m[sel] <- xy[, 1]
    pt_fit$rover_northing_utm_m[sel] <- xy[, 2]
  }
  pt_fit$crs_epsg <- crs_site
}
Show code 
# Select only relevant columns from stems dataframe
# Filter to only plots with spatial coordinates
# Multi-stemmed trees are assigned to the quadrat containing the centroid of
# their stems, so `x_quad` and `y_quad` are used to assign quadrats, while
# stem locations are kept
stem_sel <- L0$stem %>%
  left_join(., treeEquiv(L0$stem, tree_include)[, c("record_id", "tree_key")],
    by = "record_id") %>%
  dplyr::select(record_id, plot_id, tree_key, x_rel_m, y_rel_m) %>%
  filter(
    plot_id %in% L0$pt$plot_id,
    !is.na(x_rel_m),
    !is.na(y_rel_m)) %>%
  group_by(tree_key) %>%
  mutate(
    x_quad = mean(x_rel_m),
    y_quad = mean(y_rel_m)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  dplyr::select(-tree_key)
Show code 
# Extract plot corners
plot_check <- BIOMASS::plotPolygonFit(
  point_data = pt_fit,
  method = param$polygon_method,
  rel_col = c("x_rel_m", "y_rel_m"),
  proj_col = c("rover_easting_utm_m", "rover_northing_utm_m"),
  lonlat_col = NULL,
  corner_col = "corner",
  plot_col = "plot_id",
  max_dist = param$corner_outlier_dist_m,
  rm_outliers = TRUE,
  tree_data = if (nrow(stem_sel) > 0) stem_sel else NULL,
  tree_rel_col = c("x_rel_m", "y_rel_m"),
  tree_plot_col = if (nrow(stem_sel) > 0) "plot_id" else NULL,
  raster = NULL,
  shapefile = NULL,
  prop_tree = NULL,
  threshold_tree = NULL, 
  draw_plot = TRUE,
  ask = FALSE)

Next we divide the plot into 50x50 m (0.25 ha) quadrats using the BIOMASS::divide_plot() function. This function also assigns stem measurements to individual quadrats. Where a multi-stemmed tree has stems in more than one quadrat, all its stems are assigned to the quadrat containing the centroid of its stems.

Each plot is divided separately, as divide_plot() uses one grid origin for all plots. The grid is aligned by quad_origin in param.yaml: "centre" centres the grid in the plot, "corner" starts the grid at the origin corner of the plot, and a pair of numbers [x, y] starts the grid x and y m from the origin corner. Where the plot dimensions are not a multiple of the quadrat dimensions, strips along the edges of the plot are left out of the grid, e.g. with "centre", 25 m strips along each edge of a 250 x 250 m plot divided into 100 x 100 m quadrats. grid_tol, set by quad_grid_tol in param.yaml, is the maximum proportion of the plot area which may be left out of the grid. With 0.1 an error is returned if more than 10% of the plot area is not covered by the grid of quadrats. In this example the plot dimensions are a multiple of the quadrat dimensions, so no area is left out.

Show code 
# Divide plots into 50x50 m quadrats, assigning stems to quadrats using the
# centroid of their tree. divide_plot() renames `tree_coords` to `x_rel` and
# `y_rel`, so the stem coordinates are removed
tree_quad <- if (nrow(stem_sel) > 0) {
  dplyr::select(plot_check$tree_data, -x_rel, -y_rel)
} else {
  NULL
}

# Each plot is divided separately, with the quadrat grid aligned by 
# `quad_origin`
corner_coord <- as.data.frame(plot_check$corner_coord)
divide_list <- lapply(split(corner_coord, corner_coord$plot_ID), function(cc) {
  x_rng <- range(cc$x_rel)
  y_rng <- range(cc$y_rel)
  origin <- if (identical(param$quad_origin, "centre")) {
    c(x_rng[1] + (diff(x_rng) %% param$quad_dim[1]) / 2,
      y_rng[1] + (diff(y_rng) %% param$quad_dim[2]) / 2)
  } else if (identical(param$quad_origin, "corner")) {
    c(x_rng[1], y_rng[1])
  } else {
    c(x_rng[1], y_rng[1]) + param$quad_origin
  }
  td <- if (!is.null(tree_quad)) {
    tree_quad[tree_quad$plot_ID == cc$plot_ID[1], , drop = FALSE]
  } else {
    NULL
  }
  if (!is.null(td) && nrow(td) == 0) td <- NULL

  BIOMASS::divide_plot(
    corner_data = cc,
    rel_coord = c("x_rel", "y_rel"),
    proj_coord = c("x_proj", "y_proj"),
    longlat = NULL,
    grid_size = param$quad_dim,
    grid_tol = param$quad_grid_tol,
    origin = origin,
    tree_data = td,
    tree_coords = if (!is.null(td)) c("x_quad", "y_quad") else NULL,
    corner_plot_ID = "plot_ID",
    tree_plot_ID = if (!is.null(td)) "plot_ID" else NULL,
    sd_coord = NULL, 
    n = 100)
})
plot_divide <- list(
  sub_corner_coord = bind_rows(lapply(divide_list, function(x) {
    as.data.frame(x$sub_corner_coord)
  })),
  tree_data = bind_rows(lapply(divide_list, function(x) {
    if (is.null(x$tree_data)) NULL else as.data.frame(x$tree_data)
  })))

Finally, we clean up the outputs of plotPolygonFit() and divide_plot() and create sf spatial objects. We now have the following objects:

  • plot_poly - sf object with a spatial polygon for each plot.
  • quad_poly - sf object with spatial polygons for each 50x50 m quadrat.
  • stem_pt - sf object with spatial points for each stem measurement.
Show code 
# Stems outside the quadrat grid
# Stems whose tree centroid is outside the quadrat grid, by up to
# `outside_max_dist_m`, are assigned to the nearest quadrat. Others are
# excluded from quadrat summaries. In the automated workflow stems outside
# the plot are written to `report/stem_outside.csv`, so that raw data can be
# corrected if needed. Stems inside the plot, in strips left out of the 
# quadrat grid, are marked with `grid_excl`
if (nrow(stem_sel) > 0) {
  plot_divide$tree_data$grid_excl <- FALSE
  tree_dat <- plot_divide$tree_data
  quad_ext <- plot_divide$sub_corner_coord %>%
    group_by(plot_ID, subplot_ID) %>%
    summarise(
      x_min = min(x_rel), x_max = max(x_rel),
      y_min = min(y_rel), y_max = max(y_rel),
      .groups = "drop")
  plot_ext <- corner_coord %>%
    group_by(plot_ID) %>%
    summarise(
      x_min = min(x_rel), x_max = max(x_rel),
      y_min = min(y_rel), y_max = max(y_rel),
      .groups = "drop")

  # Distance from tree centroid to nearest quadrat. `x_rel` and `y_rel` in
  # the output of divide_plot() are the tree centroid
  out_idx <- which(is.na(tree_dat$subplot_ID))
  quad_near <- lapply(out_idx, function(i) {
    q <- quad_ext[quad_ext$plot_ID == tree_dat$plot_ID[i], ]
    d <- sqrt(
      pmax(q$x_min - tree_dat$x_rel[i], 0, tree_dat$x_rel[i] - q$x_max)^2 +
      pmax(q$y_min - tree_dat$y_rel[i], 0, tree_dat$y_rel[i] - q$y_max)^2)
    data.frame(quadrat_nearest = q$subplot_ID[which.min(d)], dist_m = min(d))
  })
  quad_near <- bind_rows(quad_near,
    data.frame(quadrat_nearest = character(0), dist_m = numeric(0)))

  # Whether the tree centroid is inside the plot
  pe <- plot_ext[match(tree_dat$plot_ID[out_idx], plot_ext$plot_ID), ]
  in_plot <- tree_dat$x_rel[out_idx] >= pe$x_min & 
    tree_dat$x_rel[out_idx] <= pe$x_max &
    tree_dat$y_rel[out_idx] >= pe$y_min & 
    tree_dat$y_rel[out_idx] <= pe$y_max

  stem_outside <- data.frame(
    record_id = tree_dat$record_id[out_idx],
    quadrat_nearest = quad_near$quadrat_nearest,
    dist_m = round(quad_near$dist_m, 2)) %>%
    mutate(
      action = case_when(
        dist_m <= param$outside_max_dist_m ~ "assigned to nearest quadrat",
        in_plot ~ "excluded, in plot outside quadrat grid",
        TRUE ~ "excluded"))

  # Assign stems to nearest quadrat
  assign_idx <- out_idx[stem_outside$action == "assigned to nearest quadrat"]
  plot_divide$tree_data$subplot_ID[assign_idx] <- stem_outside$quadrat_nearest[
    stem_outside$action == "assigned to nearest quadrat"]

  # Mark stems in strips left out of the quadrat grid
  grid_excl_idx <- out_idx[stem_outside$action == "excluded, in plot outside quadrat grid"]
  plot_divide$tree_data$grid_excl[grid_excl_idx] <- TRUE
}

# Create plot polygons 
plot_poly <- plot_check$polygon %>% 
  rename(plot_id = plot_ID) %>% 
  st_set_crs(crs_site) %>% 
  mutate(    
    site_id = param$site_id,
    acquisition_id = param$acquisition_id, 
    .before = everything())

# Create quadrat corner spatial points
quad_pt <- plot_divide$sub_corner_coord %>% 
  mutate(
    x_utm = x_proj,
    y_utm = y_proj) %>% 
  st_as_sf(., coords = c("x_proj", "y_proj"), crs = crs_site) %>% 
  mutate(    
    site_id = param$site_id,
    acquisition_id = param$acquisition_id, 
    .before = everything()) %>% 
  rename(
    plot_id = plot_ID, 
    quadrat_id = subplot_ID,
    x_rel_m = x_rel,
    y_rel_m = y_rel)

# Create quadrat polygons
quad_poly <- quad_pt %>% 
  group_by(site_id, acquisition_id, plot_id, quadrat_id) %>%
  summarise() %>% 
  st_convex_hull() %>%
  ungroup()

# Create stem spatial points
# Stems without coordinates are not included
if (nrow(stem_sel) > 0) {
  stem_pt <- plot_divide$tree_data %>%
    mutate(
      x_utm = x_proj,
      y_utm = y_proj) %>%
    filter(!is.na(x_proj), !is.na(y_proj)) %>%
    st_as_sf(., coords = c("x_proj", "y_proj"), crs = crs_site) %>%
    dplyr::select(
      record_id,
      quadrat_id = subplot_ID,
      grid_excl,
      x_utm, y_utm)
} else {
  stem_pt <- st_sf(
    record_id = integer(0),
    quadrat_id = character(0),
    grid_excl = logical(0),
    x_utm = numeric(0),
    y_utm = numeric(0),
    geometry = st_sfc(crs = crs_site))
}

13 Estimate quadrat AGBD and propagate error

08_agb_mc.R

Here we estimate the above-ground woody biomass density (AGBD) in each 50x50 m quadrat, with its uncertainty. The BIOMASS::AGBmonteCarlo() function propagates errors in stem diameter, wood density, height, and the AGB allometry to each stem, using Monte-Carlo simulation. The BIOMASS::subplot_summary() function then sums the simulated AGB of the stems in each quadrat and divides by the quadrat area, giving a distribution of 1000 simulated AGBD values for each quadrat.

The errors propagated depend on height_method:

  • "regional" - Equation 7 from Chave et al. (2014) is used, with the uncertainty in the environmental stress index (E) and the model parameters. Stem height is not used.
  • "field" - Equation 4 from Chave et al. (2014) is used, with stem height predicted from the local height-diameter model, including its uncertainty.

As in Estimate stem AGB, AGB is simulated for each multi-stemmed tree from its equivalent diameter, then shared among its stems in proportion to their basal area.

AGBmonteCarlo() is run on groups of whole plots, or groups of whole quadrats for very large plots, rather than on each quadrat separately. This means that quadrats containing a single tree get an uncertainty estimate, that the large diameter errors of Chave et al. (2004), applied to 5% of stems, are applied to a meaningful number of stems, and that stems outside the quadrat grid still get a stem-level uncertainty estimate.

subplot_summary() is run separately for each plot, because when plots have different numbers of quadrats and a quadrat contains no stems, subplot_summary() can assign AGBD = 0 to quadrats which contain stems.

Ideally all stems would have coordinates. Stems without coordinates in a tree where other stems have coordinates are assigned to the quadrat of the tree. Trees where no stems have coordinates are assigned to a random quadrat in their plot in each simulation, with probability proportional to quadrat area. This keeps their AGB in the plot, and adds the uncertainty in their location to the quadrat AGBD estimates. A plot where no stems have coordinates gives a similar AGBD in every quadrat, with a wider confidence interval.

A random seed is set so that the results are reproducible.

First we prepare the input dataset:

Show code 
# Define number of simulations
nsim <- 1000

# Set random seed, so results are reproducible
set.seed(42)

# Define maximum number of trees per AGBmonteCarlo() call, to limit memory use
mc_stems_max <- 10000

# Filter stem data and add quadrat IDs
stem_fil <- L0$stem %>% 
  filter(record_id %in% record_fil) %>% 
  left_join(., stem_wd_all, by = "record_id") %>% 
  left_join(., stem_height_all, by = "record_id") %>% 
  left_join(., st_drop_geometry(stem_pt)[, c("record_id", "quadrat_id", "grid_excl")], 
    by = "record_id")

if (param$height_method == "regional") {
  stem_fil <- left_join(stem_fil, p_cent, by = "plot_id")
  stopifnot(all(!is.na(stem_fil$X)))
}

# Missing wood density uncertainty would cause stems to be silently dropped
# from simulated AGB sums
stopifnot(all(!is.na(stem_fil$meanWD) & !is.na(stem_fil$sdWD)))

# Equivalent diameter of multi-stemmed trees
stem_fil <- left_join(stem_fil, treeEquiv(stem_fil, tree_include),
  by = "record_id")

# Stems of a tree share the quadrat of the tree. Stems without coordinates in
# trees with other stems that have coordinates are assigned to the quadrat of
# the tree. Trees where no stems have coordinates are assigned to quadrats at
# random below
stem_fil <- stem_fil %>%
  group_by(tree_key) %>%
  mutate(
    tree_mapped = any(!is.na(x_rel_m) & !is.na(y_rel_m)),
    quadrat_id = first(na.omit(quadrat_id)),
    # In a strip of the plot left out of the quadrat grid
    grid_excl = any(grid_excl %in% TRUE)) %>%
  ungroup()

# One row per tree. Wood density depends on taxonomic identity, which is the
# same for all stems of a tree, so the wood density of the largest stem is used
tree <- stem_fil %>%
  arrange(desc(ba_share)) %>%
  group_by(tree_key) %>%
  summarise(
    plot_id = first(plot_id),
    quadrat_id = first(quadrat_id),
    diam_eq_cm = first(diam_eq_cm),
    meanWD = first(meanWD),
    sdWD = first(sdWD),
    across(any_of(c("X", "Y")), first),
    .groups = "drop")

# Group trees into Monte Carlo chunks
# Whole plots, split into groups of whole quadrats for very large plots
quad_chunk <- tree %>%
  count(plot_id, quadrat_id) %>%
  group_by(plot_id) %>%
  mutate(mc_chunk = (cumsum(n) - 1) %/% mc_stems_max) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  dplyr::select(plot_id, quadrat_id, mc_chunk)

tree <- left_join(tree, quad_chunk, by = c("plot_id", "quadrat_id"))

tree_split <- split(tree, list(tree$plot_id, tree$mc_chunk), drop = TRUE)

Then we run the Monte-Carlo error propagation on each group of trees, and share the simulated AGB of each tree among its stems:

If repeat diameter measurements of some stems are available, a site-specific model of diameter measurement error can be estimated with BIOMASS::fitDiamError() and used instead of the model of Chave et al. (2004). The automated workflow does this if diam_error is "field", see 08_agb_mc.R. The example data have no repeat measurements, so we use the value of diam_error directly.

Show code 
# Diameter measurement error, see `diam_error` in param.yaml
diam_error <- if (identical(param$diam_error, "none")) NULL else param$diam_error

# Run AGB Monte Carlo error propagation on each chunk
tree_simu_list <- lapply(seq_along(tree_split), function(i) {
  x <- tree_split[[i]]

  # AGBmonteCarlo() fails with a single tree, so duplicate the row and keep
  # the first. Each row of `AGB_simu` is simulated independently
  n_tree <- nrow(x)
  if (n_tree == 1) {
    x <- x[c(1, 1), ]
  }

  out <- AGBmonteCarlo(
    D = x$diam_eq_cm,
    WD = x$meanWD,
    errWD = x$sdWD,
    H = NULL,
    errH = NULL,
    HDmodel = if (param$height_method == "field") height_mod else NULL,
    coord = if (param$height_method == "regional") as.matrix(x[, c("X", "Y")]) else NULL,
    Dpropag = diam_error,
    n = nsim,
    Carbon = FALSE,
    Dlim = NULL)

  out$AGB_simu[seq_len(n_tree), , drop = FALSE]
})

# Combine simulations, then share tree AGB among stems. Rows match `stem_fil`
tree <- bind_rows(tree_split)
tree_simu <- do.call(rbind, tree_simu_list)
stopifnot(nrow(tree_simu) == nrow(tree))
agb_simu <- tree_simu[match(stem_fil$tree_key, tree$tree_key), , drop = FALSE] *
  stem_fil$ba_share

# Trees where no stems have coordinates
unmapped <- !stem_fil$tree_mapped

# Stems below the minimum diameter threshold of the plot are used to estimate
# AGB, but are not included in AGB density
in_agbd <- stem_fil$record_id %in% record_agbd

# Calculate mean and standard deviation of stem AGB
# Stems used to estimate quadrat AGB density are those in a quadrat, and 
# stems of trees without coordinates if they are assigned to random quadrats
agb_Mg_mean <- rowMeans(agb_simu, na.rm = TRUE)
stem_agb_mc <- data.frame(
  record_id = stem_fil$record_id,
  agb_Mg_mean = agb_Mg_mean,
  agb_Mg_sd = sqrt(rowSums((agb_simu - agb_Mg_mean)^2, na.rm = TRUE) / 
    (rowSums(!is.na(agb_simu)) - 1)),
  quadrat_id_tree = stem_fil$quadrat_id,
  in_quadrat_calc = in_agbd & ((!unmapped & !is.na(stem_fil$quadrat_id)) |
    (unmapped & param$unmapped_method == "random")))

Then we aggregate the simulations to quadrats:

Show code 
# Format quadrat corner points
quad_pt_clean <- quad_pt %>% 
  st_drop_geometry() %>% 
  dplyr::select(
    plot_ID = plot_id,
    subplot_ID = quadrat_id,
    x_rel = x_rel_m,
    y_rel = y_rel_m,
    x_proj = x_utm,
    y_proj = y_utm)

# Area of each quadrat, from its corners in the order given by divide_plot(),
# as calculated by subplot_summary()
quad_area <- quad_pt_clean %>%
  group_by(plot_ID, subplot_ID) %>%
  summarise(
    area_ha = as.numeric(sf::st_area(sf::st_polygon(list(
      rbind(cbind(x_proj, y_proj), cbind(x_proj, y_proj)[1, ]))))) / 10000,
    .groups = "drop")

# Aggregate simulations to quadrats, separately for each plot
# Plots with no stems used to estimate AGB, e.g. plots with no trees above
# the minimum diameter threshold, have quadrats with zero AGB density
plot_vec <- unique(quad_pt_clean$plot_ID)

quad_agb_simu <- bind_rows(lapply(plot_vec, function(x) {
  quads <- quad_area[quad_area$plot_ID == x, ]

  # Stems with coordinates
  sel <- stem_fil$plot_id == x & !unmapped & in_agbd
  if (any(sel)) {
    subplots <- list(
      sub_corner_coord = quad_pt_clean[quad_pt_clean$plot_ID == x, ],
      tree_data = data.frame(
        plot_ID = x,
        subplot_ID = stem_fil$quadrat_id[sel]))

    ss <- suppressMessages(BIOMASS::subplot_summary(
      subplots = subplots,
      AGB_simu = agb_simu[sel, , drop = FALSE],
      draw_plot = FALSE))

    out <- as.data.frame(ss$long_AGB_simu) %>%
      dplyr::select(
        quadrat_id = subplot_ID,
        sim = N_simu,
        agbd_Mg_ha = AGBD)
  } else {
    out <- expand.grid(quadrat_id = quads$subplot_ID, sim = seq_len(nsim),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
    out$agbd_Mg_ha <- 0
  }

  # Trees where no stems have coordinates, assigned to a random quadrat in
  # each simulation
  # If `unmapped_method` is "exclude", they are not included in AGB density
  sel_un <- stem_fil$plot_id == x & unmapped & in_agbd
  if (param$unmapped_method == "random" && any(sel_un)) {
    agb_un <- agb_simu[sel_un, , drop = FALSE]
    # Stems of the same tree are assigned to the same quadrat
    tree_un <- stem_fil$tree_key[sel_un]
    tree_un_id <- unique(tree_un)
    quad_idx <- matrix(
      sample(nrow(quads), length(tree_un_id) * ncol(agb_un), replace = TRUE,
        prob = quads$area_ha),
      nrow = length(tree_un_id))[match(tree_un, tree_un_id), , drop = FALSE]
    # One row per quadrat, one column per simulation. matrix() keeps this
    # shape for plots with a single quadrat, where vapply() returns a vector
    agb_quad <- matrix(vapply(seq_len(ncol(agb_un)), function(j) {
      tapply(agb_un[, j], factor(quad_idx[, j], levels = seq_len(nrow(quads))), sum, default = 0)
    }, numeric(nrow(quads))), nrow = nrow(quads))
    agbd_quad <- agb_quad / quads$area_ha

    i <- cbind(match(out$quadrat_id, quads$subplot_ID), out$sim)
    out$agbd_Mg_ha <- out$agbd_Mg_ha + agbd_quad[i]
  }

  out$plot_id <- x
  out
}))

Finally extract relevant summary statistics from the AGBD error propagation:

Show code 
# Extract summary statistics from AGBD simulations
quad_agb <- quad_agb_simu %>%
  group_by(plot_id, quadrat_id) %>% 
  summarise(
    agbd_Mg_ha_mc_mean = mean(agbd_Mg_ha),
    agbd_Mg_ha_mc_median = median(agbd_Mg_ha),
    agbd_Mg_ha_mc_sd = sd(agbd_Mg_ha),
    agbd_Mg_ha_mc_ci2.5 = quantile(agbd_Mg_ha, 0.025),
    agbd_Mg_ha_mc_ci97.5 = quantile(agbd_Mg_ha, 0.975),
    .groups = "drop")
Show code 
# Visualise the distribution of AGBD estimates among quadrats, with their 95% CI
ggplot(quad_agb, aes(x = agbd_Mg_ha_mc_mean, y = reorder(quadrat_id, agbd_Mg_ha_mc_mean))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = 2) + 
  geom_point() + 
  geom_errorbar(aes(xmin = agbd_Mg_ha_mc_ci2.5, xmax = agbd_Mg_ha_mc_ci97.5), orientation = "y") + 
  theme_bw() + 
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank()) + 
  labs(
    x = expression("Above-ground woody biomass density"~(Mg~ha^-1)),
    y = "Quadrat")
Show code 
# Select top 10 highest biomass quadrats for clarity
quadrat_agb_top <- quad_agb %>% 
  slice_max(agbd_Mg_ha_mc_mean, n = 10) %>% 
  pull(quadrat_id)

# Visualise Monte-Carlo AGBD simulations for each of the top 10 quadrats with the highest AGBD 
quad_agb_simu %>% 
  filter(quadrat_id %in% quadrat_agb_top) %>% 
  ggplot(., aes(x = agbd_Mg_ha)) +
    geom_line(aes(group = quadrat_id), stat = "density", alpha = 0.8) + 
    theme_bw() + 
    labs(
      x = expression("AGBD Monte-Carlo simulations"~(Mg~ha^-1)), 
      y = "Density")

14 Compile GEO-TREES L1, L2, and L3 data products

09_stem_summ.R 10_quad_summ.R 11_brm.R

Now we have everything needed to create the GEO-TREES L1, L2 and L3 data products.

First we create a master stem table containing all the calculated values from the previous steps. This table contains many more columns than will be in the official GEO-TREES data products.

Show code 
# Combine stem dataframes
# Stems without coordinates have empty point geometries
stem_summ <- L0$stem %>%
  left_join(., stem_taxa_all, by = c("taxon_name" = "nameOriginal")) %>%
  left_join(., stem_wd_all, by = "record_id") %>%
  left_join(., stem_height_all, by = "record_id") %>%
  left_join(., stem_agb_all, by = "record_id") %>%
  left_join(., stem_agb_mc, by = "record_id") %>%
  left_join(., st_drop_geometry(stem_pt), by = "record_id") %>%
  mutate(
    # Stems without coordinates in trees with other stems that have 
    # coordinates take the quadrat of the tree
    quadrat_id = coalesce(quadrat_id_tree, quadrat_id),
    # Used to estimate AGB, and AGB density. Stems outside the quadrat grid
    # are not used to estimate AGB density
    in_agb_calc = record_id %in% record_fil,
    in_quadrat_calc = in_quadrat_calc %in% TRUE) %>%
  dplyr::select(-quadrat_id_tree) %>%
  st_as_sf(., coords = c("x_utm", "y_utm"), crs = st_crs(stem_pt),
    na.fail = FALSE, remove = FALSE)

Similarly, we create a master quadrat table, with many calculated values, more than will be in the official GEO-TREES data products.

Show code 
# Calculate area of each quadrat
quad_poly$plot_id <- as.character(quad_poly$plot_id)
quad_poly_area <- st_drop_geometry(quad_poly)
quad_poly_area$quadrat_area_ha <- as.vector(st_area(quad_poly)) * 0.0001
quad_poly_area$quadrat_dim_x_m <- param$quad_dim[1]
quad_poly_area$quadrat_dim_y_m <- param$quad_dim[2]

# Calculate quadrat summary values
quad_summ_pre <- stem_summ %>% 
  filter(in_quadrat_calc == TRUE) %>% 
  st_drop_geometry() %>% 
  group_by(site_id, acquisition_id, plot_id, quadrat_id) %>% 
  summarise(
    census_date = median(measurement_date, na.rm = TRUE),
    census_date_res = case_when(
      any(measurement_date_res == "YYYY") ~ "YYYY",
      any(measurement_date_res == "YYYY-MM") ~ "YYYY-MM",
      any(measurement_date_res == "YYYY-MM-DD") ~ "YYYY-MM-DD",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_),
    n_stem = n(),
    agb_Mg_sum = sum(agb_Mg, na.rm = TRUE),
    ba_m2_sum = sum(ba_m2, na.rm = TRUE),
    volume_m3_sum = sum(volume_m3, na.rm = TRUE),
    diam_cm_mean = mean(diam_cm, na.rm = TRUE),
    diam_cm_max = max(diam_cm, na.rm = TRUE),
    diam_cm_q80 = quantile(diam_cm, 0.8, na.rm = TRUE),
    diam_cm_q90 = quantile(diam_cm, 0.9, na.rm = TRUE),
    diam_cm_q95 = quantile(diam_cm, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE),
    height_m_pred_mean = mean(height_m_pred, na.rm = TRUE),
    height_m_pred_max_rse = height_m_pred_rse[which(height_m_pred == max(height_m_pred, na.rm = TRUE))][1],
    height_m_pred_max = max(height_m_pred, na.rm = TRUE),
    height_m_pred_q80 = quantile(height_m_pred, 0.8, na.rm = TRUE),
    height_m_pred_q90 = quantile(height_m_pred, 0.9, na.rm = TRUE),
    height_m_pred_q95 = quantile(height_m_pred, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE),
    lorey_height_m = sum(ba_m2 * height_m_pred, na.rm = TRUE) / 
      sum(ba_m2[!is.na(height_m_pred)], na.rm = TRUE),
    meanWD_mean = mean(meanWD, na.rm = TRUE),
    meanWD_wm_ba = weighted.mean(meanWD, ba_m2, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop_last") %>% 
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    across(
      .cols = where(~inherits(.x, "units")), 
      .fns = as.vector),
    # max() of only NAs returns -Inf
    across(
      .cols = where(is.numeric), 
      .fns = ~replace(.x, is.infinite(.x), NA_real_))) 
  
# Add quadrat polygons, fill in quadrats with no trees
quad_summ <- quad_poly %>% 
  left_join(., quad_poly_area, 
    by = c("site_id", "acquisition_id", "plot_id", "quadrat_id")) %>% 
  left_join(., quad_summ_pre, 
    by = c("site_id", "acquisition_id", "plot_id", "quadrat_id")) %>% 
  # Quadrat AGBD from error propagation, including stems without coordinates
  left_join(., quad_agb, by = c("plot_id", "quadrat_id")) %>%
  mutate(
    empty_quadrat = is.na(n_stem),
    across(
      c(
        any_of(c(
          "n_stem", 
          "ba_m2_sum",
          "volume_m3_sum",
          "agb_Mg_sum")),
        starts_with("agbd_Mg_ha_mc_")), 
      ~if_else(empty_quadrat & is.na(.x), 0, .x)),
    across(
      c(
        all_of("n_stem"),
        starts_with(c("ba_m2_", "volume_m3_", "agb_Mg"))),
      ~.x / quadrat_area_ha,
      .names = "{.col}_ha")) %>% 
  dplyr::select(-empty_quadrat)

Then we can create the L1, L2 and L3 GEO-TREES tree inventory data products.

Each data product has an associated RO-Crate manifest file in the same directory (*_ro-crate-metadata.json), which records the version of the code and the input data sources so they can be reproduced. These files are created programmatically in R using the rocrateR package. The RO-Crate format is flexible so you can add additional information as needed to reproduce the output data product.

Below is the contents of an example RO-Crate file for the L3 tree inventory (INV) quadrat-level AGBD estimates. It specifies the input data, the version of the INV_processing GitHub repository containing the code, and the output data product. It includes meta-data describing each input and output dataset, meta-data on who executed the workflow and when.

Show code 
rocrate_example <- rocrateR::read_rocrate("./data-raw/data/ro-crate-metadata.json")

print(rocrate_example)

For the tree inventory data we also include a copy of the param.yaml file to record the parameters used by that PRODUCTVERSION.

These are the official GEO-TREES tree inventory data products:

  • L1 re-formatted stem measurements.
  • L1 re-formatted plot geo-location points
  • L1 re-formatted plot meta-data
  • L2 stem AGB estimates.
  • L2 plot polygons.
  • L3 AGBD estimates within plot quadrats.

First we create the data objects.

Show code 
L1_stem <- stem_summ %>% 
  st_transform(., 4326) %>% 
  bind_cols(., st_coordinates(.)) %>% 
  st_drop_geometry() %>% 
  dplyr::select(
    BRM_site = site_id,
    Acquisition = acquisition_id,
    Plot_name = plot_id,
    Measurement_date = measurement_date,
    Tree_label = tree_id,
    Stem_label = stem_id,
    Botany_genus = genusAccepted,
    Botany_species = speciesAccepted,
    Botany_author = authorAccepted,
    Botany_family = familyAccepted,
    Position_x = x_rel_m,
    Position_y = y_rel_m,
    Longitude = X,
    Latitude = Y,
    Diameter = diam_cm,
    POM = pom_m,
    Total_height = height_m,
    Code = code)

# Prepare L1 GNSS dataset
L1_pt <- L0$pt

# Prepare L1 plot meta-data 
L1_plot <- L0$plot

# Prepare L2 stems dataset
L2_stem <- stem_summ %>% 
  filter(in_quadrat_calc == TRUE) %>% 
  st_transform(., 4326) %>% 
  bind_cols(., st_coordinates(.)) %>% 
  st_drop_geometry() %>% 
  mutate(
    agb_Mg_mean = ifelse(is.na(agb_Mg_mean), agb_Mg, agb_Mg_mean)) %>% 
  dplyr::select(
    BRM_site = site_id,
    Acquisition = acquisition_id,
    Plot_name = plot_id,
    Measurement_date = measurement_date,
    Tree_label = tree_id,
    Stem_label = stem_id,
    Longitude = X,
    Latitude = Y,
    WD_stem_estimate = meanWD,
    WD_stem_uncertainty = sdWD,
    AGB_tree_estimate = agb_Mg_mean,
    AGB_tree_uncertainty = agb_Mg_sd,
    Height_stem_estimate = height_m_pred,
    Height_stem_uncertainty = height_m_pred_rse)

# Prepare L2 plot polygons dataset 
L2_poly <- plot_poly %>% 
  dplyr::select(
    BRM_site = site_id,
    Acquisition = acquisition_id,
    Plot_name = plot_id)

# Check all values filled
stopifnot(all(!is.na(L2_stem$AGB_tree_estimate)))
stopifnot(all(!is.na(L2_stem$AGB_tree_uncertainty)))

# Prepare L3 quadrat dataset
# Select parameters to copy as columns
param_fil <- param
param_fil$quadrat_dim_x_m <- param_fil$quad_dim[1]
param_fil$quadrat_dim_y_m <- param_fil$quad_dim[2]
param_fil[["quad_dim"]] <- NULL
if (param_fil$opt_s3) { 
  param_fil[["raw_dir"]] <- param_fil$s3_dir
} 
param_fil[c("site_id", "acquisition_id", "out_dir", "quad_dim", "s3_dir", "opt_s3", "rocrate", "als_date", "quad_origin")] <- NULL

L3_quad <- quad_summ %>% 
  dplyr::select(
    BRM_site = site_id,
    Acquisition = acquisition_id,
    Plot_name = plot_id,
    Census_date = census_date,
    Quadrat_name = quadrat_id,
    AGBD_stand_estimate = agbd_Mg_ha_mc_mean,
    AGBD_stand_uncertainty = agbd_Mg_ha_mc_sd,
    Height_stand_estimate = height_m_pred_max,
    Height_stand_uncertainty = height_m_pred_max_rse,
    Basal_area = ba_m2_sum_ha,
    Lorey_height = lorey_height_m,
    Wood_density = meanWD_wm_ba,
    Quadrat_area = quadrat_area_ha) %>%
  bind_cols(param_fil)

# Check all values filled
stopifnot(all(!is.na(L3_quad$AGBD_stand_estimate)))

# Check not all AGBD estimates should be zero
stopifnot(!all(L3_quad$AGBD_stand_estimate == 0))

Then we create the filenames and output directories for the data objects, which are a concatenation of the following values, matching the order of the GEO-TREES directory hierarchy.

Show code 
# Create sanitised software version string for filenames
software_version_sanit <- gsub("\\.", "-", param$software_version)

# Construct output filenames
L1_filename <- paste(
    param$site_id, 
    "INV", 
    param$acquisition_id, 
    param$product_version,
    software_version_sanit, 
    "L1", 
  sep = "_")

L2_filename <- paste(
    param$site_id, 
    "INV", 
    param$acquisition_id, 
    param$product_version,
    software_version_sanit, 
    "L2", 
  sep = "_")

L3_filename <- paste(
    param$site_id, 
    "INV", 
    param$acquisition_id, 
    param$product_version,
    software_version_sanit, 
    "L3", 
  sep = "_")

# Create output directories
L_list <- c("L1", "L2", "L3")
L_dir_list <- lapply(L_list, function(x) { 
  file.path(param$out_dir, software_version_sanit, x)
})
names(L_dir_list) <- L_list

Then we can write the data objects to files:

Show code 
lapply(L_dir_list, dir.create, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

# Write L1 dataset to file
write.csv(L1_stem, file.path(L_dir_list[["L1"]], paste0(L1_filename, "_stem", ".csv")), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(L1_plot, file.path(L_dir_list[["L1"]], paste0(L1_filename, "_plot", ".csv")), row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(L1_pt, file.path(L_dir_list[["L1"]], paste0(L1_filename, "_pt", ".csv")), row.names = FALSE)

# Write L2 dataset to file
write.csv(L2_stem, file.path(L_dir_list[["L2"]], paste0(L2_filename, "_stem", ".csv")), row.names = FALSE)
st_write(L2_poly , file.path(L_dir_list[["L2"]], paste0(L2_filename, "_poly", ".gpkg")), delete_dsn = TRUE) 

# Write L3 dataset to file
st_write(L3_quad, file.path(L_dir_list[["L3"]], paste0(L3_filename, "_quad", ".gpkg")), delete_dsn = TRUE)

Finally, we can construct the RO-Crate files which sit alongside each data product. The author, affiliation, and license are taken from the rocrate section of param.yaml. If author_orcid is provided, it is used as the identifier of the author.

Show code 
# Construct RO-crates
# Author, affiliation and license are defined in param.yaml

# Create local RO-Crate identifier from a name
rocrateId <- function(x) {
  paste0("#", gsub("^-|-$", "", gsub("[^a-z0-9]+", "-", tolower(x))))
}

# Author, identified by ORCID if provided
me <- entity(
  x = if (!is.null(param$rocrate$author_orcid)) {
    param$rocrate$author_orcid 
  } else { 
    rocrateId(param$rocrate$author_name)
  },
  type = "Person",
  name = param$rocrate$author_name,
  email = param$rocrate$author_email
)

# Affiliation
aff <- entity(
  x = rocrateId(param$rocrate$affiliation),
  type = "Organization",
  name = param$rocrate$affiliation
)

# License
lic <- entity(
  x = param$rocrate$license,
  type = c("File", "CreativeWork") 
)

# Input directory
indir <- entity(
  x = paste0(param$raw_dir, "/"),
  type = "Dataset",
  description = "Directory containing raw L0 data."
)

# Output files
L1_stem_outfile <- entity(
  x = file.path(L_dir_list[["L1"]], paste0(L1_filename, "_stem", ".csv")),
  type = "File",
  description = "L1 re-formatted stem measurements.",
  encodingFormat = "text/csv"
)

L1_pt_outfile <- entity(
  x = file.path(L_dir_list[["L1"]], paste0(L1_filename, "_pt", ".csv")),
  type = "File",
  description = "L1 re-formatted plot geo-location points",
  encodingFormat = "text/csv"
)

L1_plot_outfile <- entity(
  x = file.path(L_dir_list[["L1"]], paste0(L1_filename, "_plot", ".csv")),
  type = "File",
  description = "L1 re-formatted plot meta-data",
  encodingFormat = "text/csv"
)

L2_stem_outfile <- entity(
  x = file.path(L_dir_list[["L2"]], paste0(L2_filename, "_stem", ".csv")),
  type = "File",
  description = "L2 stem AGB estimates.",
  encodingFormat = "text/csv"
)

L2_poly_outfile <- entity(
  x = file.path(L_dir_list[["L2"]], paste0(L2_filename, "_poly", ".gpkg")),
  type = "File",
  description = "L2 plot polygons.",
  encodingFormat = "application/geopackage+sqlite3"
)


L3_quad_outfile <- entity(
  x = file.path(L_dir_list[["L3"]], paste0(L3_filename, "_quad", ".gpkg")),
  type = "File",
  description = "L3 AGBD estimates within plot quadrats.",
  encodingFormat = "application/geopackage+sqlite3"
)

# Parameters file
yaml <- entity(
  x = "param.yaml",
  type = "File",
  description = "Configuration parameters.",
  encodingFormat = "application/yaml"
)

# Software 
code <- entity(
  x = paste0("#INV_processing_", param$software_version),
  type = c("SoftwareApplication", "SoftwareSourceCode"),
  name = "GEO-TREES AGBD processing pipeline",
  version = param$software_version,
  url = paste0("https://github.com/GEO-TREES/INV_processing/releases/tag/", param$software_version),
  programmingLanguage = "R"
)

# Execution action
exec <- entity(
  x = "#run-tree_inventory_pipeline",
  type = "CreateAction",
  name = "Tree inventory pipeline execution",
  description = "Execute tree inventory pipeline to generate data products",
  endTime = strftime(Sys.time(), format = "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ", tz = "UTC")
)

L_outfile_list <- list(
  "L1" = list(
    "L1_stem" = L1_stem_outfile,
    "L1_plot" = L1_plot_outfile,
    "L1_pt" = L1_pt_outfile
  ),
  "L2" = list(
    "L2_stem" = L2_stem_outfile,
    "L2_poly" = L2_poly_outfile
  ),
  "L3" = list(
    "L3_quad" = L3_quad_outfile
  )
)

# Initialize crates, add entities and relationships
rocrate_list <- lapply(names(L_outfile_list), function(x) { 
  rc <- rocrate(
    context = "https://w3id.org/ro/crate/1.2/context",
    datePublished = as.character(Sys.Date()),
    name = paste("GEO-TREES", param$site_id, "INV", x)
  ) %>%
    add_entity(me) %>%
    add_entity(aff) %>%
    add_entity(lic) %>%
    add_entity(indir) %>%
    add_entity(yaml) %>%
    add_entity(code) %>%
    add_entity(exec)

  for (i in L_outfile_list[[x]]) {
    rc <- rc %>% add_entity(i)
  }

  L_outfile_id_list <- unname(lapply(L_outfile_list[[x]], function(i) { 
    list(`@id` = i$`@id`) 
  }))

  rc %>%
    add_entity_value(id = "./", key = "author", value = list(`@id` = me$`@id`)) %>%
    add_entity_value(id = "./", key = "license", value = list(`@id` = lic$`@id`)) %>%
    add_entity_value(id = "./", key = "hasPart", 
      value = c(
        list(
          list(`@id` = yaml$`@id`),
          list(`@id` = indir$`@id`),
          list(`@id` = lic$`@id`)
        ),
        L_outfile_id_list
      )
    ) %>%
    add_entity_value(id = "./", key = "mentions", value = list(
        list(`@id` = exec$`@id`),
        list(`@id` = code$`@id`)
      )) %>%
    add_entity_value(id = me$`@id`, key = "affiliation", value = list(`@id` = aff$`@id`)) %>%
    add_entity_value(id = exec$`@id`, key = "object", 
      value = list(
        list(`@id` = yaml$`@id`),
        list(`@id` = indir$`@id`)
      )) %>%
    add_entity_value(id = exec$`@id`, key = "result", value = L_outfile_id_list) %>%
    add_entity_value(id = exec$`@id`, key = "instrument", value = list(`@id` = code$`@id`))
})
names(rocrate_list) <- names(L_outfile_list)
Show code 
# Write crates to file
lapply(names(rocrate_list), function(x) { 
  write_rocrate(rocrate_list[[x]], 
    file.path(L_dir_list[[x]], "ro-crate-metadata.json"))
})

# Copy param.yaml to each data output
lapply(L_dir_list, function(x) { 
  file.copy("./param.yaml", file.path(x, "param.yaml"))
})

15 Next steps

The L3 tree inventory data product is passed to the AGBD geo-spatial modelling workflow to produce landscape-level estimates of AGBD at 50x50 m gridded resolution, in combination with the ALS L3 data products.
